fields.title: Smena: retention is falling, six hypotheses
fields.summary: Everyone on the team is confident in their theory. Decide how to find the real cause.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you investigate the cause, and in what order?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Smena.
fields.brief/company: Smena is a shift scheduling service for small cafes and stores: 2,100 paying accounts.
fields.brief/context: Day 30 retention dropped from 44% to 38% over six months. Six hypotheses were voiced at the meeting. The founder asks for a plan by Monday. The analyst is available for two days, the researcher for three.
fields.brief/objective: Understand what is really happening before the team wastes a sprint.
fields.brief/constraints: One week. Two days of analyst time, three days of researcher time, engineering is fully booked until the end of the month.
fields.brief/task: Decide how you will investigate the cause and explain the sequence of steps.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: First check whether the audience composition changed
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Any aggregate metric is a mix of behavior and audience composition. When acquisition increases significantly, the average drops even if retention improves in every subgroup, and the team starts fixing what is already working. A cohort breakdown takes an hour and either confirms the issue or eliminates half the theories at once—which is why it comes first, before any interviews or engineering work.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Day 30 retention: 44% → 38% over six months.

Over the same period, marketing ramped up acquisition: 210 new accounts per month instead of 90.

The analyst noted: "I haven't done a breakdown by registration cohorts yet—let me know if needed. I have breakdowns by platform, app version, account size, and channel; each takes an hour to run."

Additionally: the share of accounts where at least one employee opened the schedule is 61%. Six months ago it was 63%.

The number of published schedules per week per active account stayed flat: 1.0.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Founder: "a competitor lowered their price."
Marketing: "seasonality; cafes hire less during summer."
Support: "the main screen redesign made things confusing."
Engineering: "the app started lagging on older Android devices."
Sales: "we started selling to the wrong audience—targeting accounts that are too small."
Founder again: "people simply don't understand the value, we need onboarding."

They discussed this for forty minutes and started checking the founder's theory about the competitor—only to find the competitor hadn't changed prices.

Not a single hypothesis was formulated in a way that could be ruled out by data.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Notes from past interviews, never synthesized:

— Four out of seven owners call or message employees after publishing a schedule to confirm they saw it. This takes 10–20 minutes a week.
— Two continue keeping a parallel schedule in phone notes while claiming they "love everything."
— One said: "I switched when a barista didn't show up on Saturday because he missed a shift swap in the chat."

There is no data on churn reasons: churned users have never been interviewed.

The product lacks an event for "employee opened the schedule"—there is only "notification sent."
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What can be done in a week
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Analyst: registration cohort breakdown takes an hour. Breakdowns by platform, version, account size, and channel take an hour each.

Researcher: in three days, conducting 5–6 interviews is realistic if candidates exist; the list of churned contacts can be pulled in an hour.

Engineering is fully booked until the end of the month, except for minor tasks under one day.

Paying accounts model: accounts × active share × schedule-closing share × renewal rate. Values for all four multipliers are in analytics.

Tracking "employee opened schedule" takes two engineering days and has been sitting in the backlog for three months.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Decompose the metric and eliminate theories with breakdowns
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: First, analyze retention by registration cohort, then slice by platform, version, and account size, checking any remaining branches through researcher interviews.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The cohort breakdown takes an hour and flips the narrative: within each monthly cohort, retention actually grew from 41% to 47%. The aggregate decline is explained by the share of new accounts doubling, and new accounts always have lower retention.
This means the product did not get worse. The hypotheses about the redesign, lag, competitor, and seasonality fall away—they would have predicted a drop within cohorts.
That leaves the sales hypothesis: acquiring accounts that are too small. A breakdown by size confirms it: single-location accounts have 29% retention compared to 52% for others, and their share has grown.
Three calls with churned single-location owners reveal the mechanism: single-shift schedules are kept in memory, making the product unnecessary.
By Monday, the team doesn't have a list of theories, but a single conclusion and a decision on whom to sell to.
Trade-off: half a day of analyst time and letting go of five hypotheses championed by respected people.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Give three days to the researcher for interviews
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: There is plenty of data, but no understanding. Conduct 5–6 calls with churned users to uncover the cause directly.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The churned user list is pulled in an hour, and four people are reached.
The conversations are useful: two are single-location owners who say a single-shift schedule is kept in their head. One complains about not knowing if an employee saw a replacement shift. One left due to price.
This points in the right direction, but the scale isn't measured: it's unclear whether this represents a quarter of the user base or three percent. By Monday, the conclusion sounds like "there are several reasons," and debate over the main one continues.
The cohort breakdown—which would have taken an hour and answered whether the product worsened at all—was never done.
Trade-off: you uncovered mechanisms without understanding their scale, using up the week's scarcest resource.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Build onboarding as suggested by the founder
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The theory about misunderstanding value sounds plausible and is easiest to test by building. Put onboarding into development.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Engineering is booked until the end of the month, so onboarding starts next month and launches six weeks later.
Aggregate retention stays unchanged. Later, a cohort breakdown shows that retention within cohorts was already growing, while the average dropped due to the acquisition spike.
This hypothesis took longer to test than all others combined and was distinguished from the six only by who proposed it.
Trade-off: you spent a month and a half on the most expensive test of an ordinary hunch.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Use the growth model to estimate where the impact is largest
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Values for all four multipliers are available. Calculate which one is most sensitive and focus on it.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The calculation takes half an hour and proves useful: the schedule-closing share is the most sensitive multiplier; improving it by a quarter yields more than a similar improvement in the others.
However, the model answers "where to focus," not "what happened." It doesn't explain the retention drop, leaving the acquisition spike hypothesis untested.
The team tackles the schedule-closing share, but the founder's question—"why did retention drop?"—remains open and resurfaces a month later.
Trade-off: you identified a solid roadmap priority, but failed to answer the question asked.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The customer is described through demographics rather than jobs and pain points
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Collected findings were not synthesized, leaving blind spots hidden
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Behavior is explained by persona profile rather than situation
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Failed to identify how the person currently solves the task and why that habit persists
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The end-to-end journey was not considered: steps outside the product remained invisible
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: The root cause is sought at the storefront, though it originates in back-of-house processes
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Hypotheses are shuffled in circles instead of decomposing metrics and breakdowns
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: An aggregate metric is evaluated without cohorts, even though audience composition is changing
fields.rubric/remediation/8/gap: Effect size was not estimated prior to execution
